title: ser and estar
intro: Both verbs mean “to be”. Ser says what something is or what it is like. Estar says where it is and what state it is in right now.

variants.mx: Mexicans often put bien before an adjective as an intensifier (está bien bonito = it is really nice, es bien fácil = it is really easy).
variants.es: Ser and estar work the same in Spain. To intensify an adjective Spain rather uses muy or, colloquially, súper (está muy bonito, es súper fácil); bien in this sense sounds Latin American.

rules.title: Who or what it is
rules.text: A name, a relationship, a nationality, and also who someone used to be (de niño = as a child).
rules.because: It says who or what it is, so ser.
examples: When I was a kid, I lived in Puebla.

rules.title: Origin
rules.text: Where someone or something is from: ser de.
rules.because: It's about origin (where someone is from), so ser.

rules.title: Profession
rules.text: Without an article: soy maestro, not soy un maestro.
rules.because: It's about a profession, so ser.
examples: I used to be a waiter.

rules.title: Characteristics, description
rules.text: What something is like in general: character, looks, color, size, price, opinion.
rules.because: It describes what something is like in general, so ser.

rules.title: Time and date
rules.text: Hours, days, dates. For one o'clock it's es la una, otherwise son las…
rules.because: It's about the time or the date, so ser.

rules.title: Whose it is, what it's made of
rules.text: Ser de + the owner or the material.
rules.because: It says whose it is or what it's made of, so ser.
examples: The table is made of wood.

rules.title: Where and when something takes place
rules.text: An event (fiesta, examen, junta) “takes place”, so it's ser even though it's about a place.
rules.because: It says when or where something takes place, so ser.
examples: The party is at my house.
The exam will be on Monday.

rules.title: Location
rules.text: Where someone or something is.
rules.because: It's about where someone or something is, so estar.

rules.title: State, mood, health
rules.text: How someone is doing or what something is like right now. That includes how something tastes.
rules.because: It's about a state or a mood right now, so estar.

rules.title: The result of an action
rules.text: A state that came out of something. Often a participle in -ado, -ido: cerrado, casado, dormido.
rules.because: It's a state that results from an action, so estar.

rules.title: Fixed expressions
rules.text: Some phrases have to be learned whole: estar de acuerdo, estar en oferta, estar de vacaciones.
rules.because: It's a fixed expression with estar.

rules.title: An action in progress
rules.text: Estar + gerund (-ando, -iendo).
rules.because: The action is in progress (estar + gerund), so estar.

title: Present tense (presente)
intro: It covers what you do regularly and what you are doing right now. The ending changes with the person, and the pronoun (yo, tú…) is usually left out.

variants.mx: Mexico always uses ustedes for several people (ustedes hablan); the vosotros form (habláis) is not heard there. For one person it always uses tú; voseo (vos hablás) survives only in a few southern states, for example Chiapas. Mexicans also say the subject pronoun more often (Yo estudio español).
variants.es: In Spain several people you would call tú are vosotros (vosotros habláis, coméis, vivís). Ustedes (ustedes hablan) is the polite form, for people you would call usted. Every verb table shows the vosotros form.

rules.title: When it is used
rules.text: What you do regularly (siempre, todos los días, los lunes), what is always true, and in Mexico often the near future too: Mañana te llamo.
examples: I take the bus every day.

rules.title: Verbs in -ar
rules.text: hablar: hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan.

rules.title: Verbs in -er and -ir
rules.text: comer: como, comes, come, comemos, comen. vivir: vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, viven.

rules.title: Stem changes
rules.text: In some verbs the vowel changes: e → ie (querer: quiero), o → ue (poder: puedo), e → i (pedir: pido). It doesn't change in the nosotros form: queremos, podemos, pedimos.

rules.title: Irregular yo
rules.text: Some verbs are irregular only in the yo form: tengo, hago, salgo, pongo, digo, vengo, sé, conozco, doy, veo.

rules.title: Fully irregular
rules.text: ser: soy, eres, es, somos, son. estar: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están. ir: voy, vas, va, vamos, van.

title: Preterite (pretérito)
intro: It tells of something that happened and is over: yesterday, last week, once. In Mexico it's the everyday past tense for recent events too, where English might say “I have eaten”.

variants.mx: In Mexico the pretérito is the usual tense for today and the recent past too (hoy desayuné temprano), where Spain often says he desayunado.
variants.es: In Spain the pretérito is the tense for yesterday and earlier (ayer desayuné temprano). For today and the recent past Spain says the present perfect: hoy he desayunado temprano. The vosotros form: hablasteis, comisteis.

rules.title: When it is used
rules.text: Something that happened and finished at a set time: ayer, anoche, el lunes, la semana pasada, en 2020, una vez. Descriptions and habits in the past take the imperfecto.
examples: Yesterday I chatted with my grandma.
Last year we went to Oaxaca.
I didn't sleep well last night.

rules.title: Verbs in -ar
rules.text: hablar: hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablaron. The accent on the ending matters: hablo = I speak, habló = he spoke.
examples: Yesterday I talked to my mom.

rules.title: Verbs in -er and -ir
rules.text: comer: comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comieron. vivir: viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivieron.
examples: Did you go out last night?

rules.title: Irregular stem
rules.text: These verbs have a different stem and endings without an accent (-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron): tener → tuve, estar → estuve, poder → pude, hacer → hice (hizo), venir → vine, decir → dije (dijeron).

rules.title: ser and ir share their forms
rules.text: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron. The rest of the sentence tells you which one it is.
examples: It was a very nice day.

rules.title: Spelling change in the yo form
rules.text: To keep the pronunciation: -car → -qué (busqué), -gar → -gué (llegué), -zar → -cé (empecé).

rules.title: A change only in the él and ellos forms
rules.text: Stem-changing -ir verbs change in the preterite only in the third person: e → i (pedir: pidió, pidieron), o → u (dormir: durmió, durmieron). Between two vowels, i becomes y: leer → leyó, leyeron.

title: Imperfect (imperfecto)
intro: It describes what used to happen or what things were like: what you used to do, how it was, how old you were.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere. The vosotros form: hablabais, comíais, erais, ibais.

rules.title: When it is used
rules.text: A habit (siempre, todos los días, antes), a description in the past, age and time. English often says “used to” or “was …ing”.
examples: I used to work at a bank.

rules.title: Verbs in -ar
rules.text: hablar: hablaba, hablabas, hablaba, hablábamos, hablaban. The yo and él forms are the same.
examples: As a kid I used to play in the street.

rules.title: Verbs in -er and -ir
rules.text: comer: comía, comías, comía, comíamos, comían. vivir: vivía, vivías, vivía, vivíamos, vivían.

rules.title: Only three irregular verbs
rules.text: ser: era, eras, era, éramos, eran. ir: iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, iban. ver: veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veían.
examples: When I was a kid, I walked to school.

title: Preterite or imperfect?
intro: Both are past tenses. The preterite says what happened. The imperfect says what things were like at the time, or what happened again and again.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere: pretérito for a finished event, imperfecto for description and habit.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere: pretérito for a finished event, imperfecto for description and habit. For today Spain adds he comido, see the present perfect.

rules.title: One completed event → preterite
rules.text: Words like ayer, anoche, el lunes, una vez, hace dos años.
examples: Yesterday I went to the doctor.
I lived in Mexico for two years.

rules.title: Habit and repetition → imperfect
rules.text: Words like siempre, todos los días, cada verano, de niño, antes.
examples: We used to go to the beach every summer.

rules.title: Description and background → imperfect
rules.text: What the weather was like, how someone felt, what time it was, what was going on.
examples: It was cold and I was tired.

rules.title: Both in one sentence
rules.text: The imperfect is the background; the preterite is what suddenly happened.
examples: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
When we arrived, the hotel was already full.

title: Ir a + infinitive (going to)
intro: The most common way to say what I am going to do: a form of ir + a + infinitive. Voy a estudiar = I am going to study.

variants.mx: In Mexico it is the usual way to talk about the future, even the more distant one (el próximo año voy a vivir en Monterrey). Sometimes it also means what I am about to do right now (voy a hablar con él = I'm going to talk to him).
variants.es: Spain uses ir a + infinitive a lot too, but the -ré future is heard more often in speech there than in Latin America. The vosotros form: vais a (vais a comer).

rules.title: voy a, vas a, va a…
rules.text: Only ir changes (voy, vas, va, vamos, van); a and the infinitive stay: voy a comer, vamos a salir.
rules.because: Ir is conjugated for the person, followed by a + infinitive: voy a, vas a, va a, vamos a, van a.
examples: What are you going to do on Saturday?

rules.title: Plans and the near future
rules.text: What I plan or what is about to happen: mañana voy a trabajar, va a llover. In Mexico it is also used for the more distant future.
rules.because: It is a plan or something about to happen, so ir a + infinitive.
examples: We're going to travel in May.
Look at those clouds, it's going to rain.

rules.title: The pronoun before ir or at the end
rules.text: The pronoun can go before the form of ir or be attached to the infinitive: lo voy a hacer = voy a hacerlo.
rules.because: The pronoun goes before the form of ir or is attached to the end of the infinitive.
examples: I'm going to do it tomorrow.
I'm going to call you tonight.

title: Future tense (futuro)
intro: The endings are added to the whole infinitive and are the same for all verbs. Plans are more often said with ir a + infinitive in speech (tip Ir a + infinitive).

variants.mx: Mexicans talk about plans mostly with ir a (voy a viajar). The futuro is often used for a guess (¿qué hora será? = what time might it be?).
variants.es: Spain too talks about plans mostly with ir a (voy a viajar), and the futuro is also used for a guess (¿qué hora será?). The vosotros form: hablaréis, tendréis.

rules.title: When it is used
rules.text: Predictions, promises and plans for later (el próximo año, algún día). It sounds surer and more formal than ir a + infinitive.
examples: Next year I will live in Guadalajara.
Tomorrow it will rain in the afternoon.
I promise, I will be on time.

rules.title: Infinitive + ending
rules.text: hablar: hablaré, hablarás, hablará, hablaremos, hablarán. Likewise comeré, viviré.
examples: Tomorrow I will talk to the boss.

rules.title: Irregular stem
rules.text: The endings stay, the stem changes: tener → tendré, poder → podré, salir → saldré, venir → vendré, poner → pondré, decir → diré, hacer → haré, querer → querré, saber → sabré.
examples: I will have time on Saturday.

rules.title: A guess
rules.text: The future tense also expresses a guess about the present.

title: Present progressive (estar + gerundio)
intro: It says what is happening at this very moment. It is made of the verb estar and a gerund, like English “I am working”.

variants.mx: Mexicans use the progressive a lot, often with ahorita (ahorita estoy comiendo = I am eating right now). Careful: in Mexico ahorita also means “later, at some point” (ahorita lo hago = I will do it when I get to it). It is also used for a single moment: está viniendo = he is arriving right now (Spain says viene).
variants.es: Spain uses the progressive somewhat less than Mexico. Ahorita is not heard there; Spain says ahora mismo (ahora mismo estoy comiendo = I am eating right now).

rules.title: When the present is enough
rules.text: Spanish uses it less than English does: for habits and for the near future it's the plain present, not the progressive.

rules.title: estar + gerund
rules.text: Only estar is conjugated: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están. The gerund doesn't change.

rules.title: How the gerund is formed
rules.text: -ar → -ando (hablar: hablando), -er and -ir → -iendo (comer: comiendo, vivir: viviendo).

rules.title: Irregular gerunds
rules.text: leer → leyendo, ir → yendo, dormir → durmiendo, pedir → pidiendo, decir → diciendo.

title: Gender of nouns
intro: Every noun is masculine (el) or feminine (la), things included. English has nothing like it, but the ending often tells you which it is.

variants.mx: In American Spanish some words are used in another gender too: el sartén beside la sartén, el radio beside la radio (the RAE lists both genders for both words), in part of Mexico also el costumbre. When unsure, follow the dictionary.
variants.es: Some words have a different gender in Spain than in Mexico: la radio (the broadcast and the set), la sartén (frying pan).

rules.title: -o is masculine, -a is feminine
rules.text: True for most words.

rules.title: Feminine endings
rules.text: -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad, -umbre.

rules.title: Masculine endings
rules.text: -or, -aje and most words in -ma that come from Greek.

rules.title: Exceptions worth knowing
rules.text: La foto and la moto are feminine too (short for fotografía, motocicleta).

rules.title: People
rules.text: The gender follows the person. The ending -o becomes -a; after a consonant, -a is added.

rules.title: el before a stressed a-
rules.text: Feminine words that start with a stressed a- or ha- take the article el in the singular. They stay feminine.

title: Articles (el, la, un, una)
intro: Spanish uses articles more often than English does. The article agrees with its noun in gender and number.

variants.mx: In Mexico the article stands before casa where Spain does without it: Vamos a la casa (Spain rather Vamos a casa). In writing a name takes no article (María, Juan).
variants.es: In Spain a name usually stands without an article (María, Juan). La María, el Juan sounds colloquial; in some regions (Catalonia, for one) it is common.

rules.title: Definite article: el, la, los, las
rules.text: For something specific or already known, and also when you talk about things in general, where English uses no article.

rules.title: Indefinite article: un, una, unos, unas
rules.text: For something you mention for the first time or that is one of many.

rules.title: al and del
rules.text: a + el = al, de + el = del. La, los and las never contract.

rules.title: Days and hours
rules.text: el lunes = on Monday, los lunes = on Mondays. Hours take la or las.
examples: On Monday I have a meeting.

rules.title: When there is no article
rules.text: With a profession after ser, where English says “a”, and with an unspecified amount.

title: Adjective agreement
intro: An adjective takes the gender and number of its noun and usually comes after it. In English it never changes; in Spanish it almost always does.

variants.mx: Mexicans use diminutives in -ito/-ita a lot, with adjectives and adverbs too (chiquito, despacito, ahorita).
variants.es: Spain uses diminutives too (un momentito, un cafecito), in some regions also in -illo, -ín (un poquillo, pequeñín). Ahorita is not used there.

rules.title: -o / -a
rules.text: Adjectives in -o have a feminine form in -a.

rules.title: One form for both genders
rules.text: Adjectives that end in -e or in a consonant don't change with gender.

rules.title: Plural
rules.text: After a vowel add -s, after a consonant -es.

rules.title: After ser and estar too
rules.text: The adjective agrees with whoever or whatever it is about.

rules.title: Word order
rules.text: First the noun, then the adjective. Words like mucho, poco, otro go before it. Bueno and malo shorten to buen, mal before a masculine noun.

title: Reflexive verbs
intro: The infinitive ends in -se (levantarse). The pronoun changes with the person: me, te, se, nos, se.

variants.mx: Some verbs are reflexive more often in Mexico than elsewhere (regresarse = to go back, tardarse = to take long). Likewise desayunarse (to have breakfast) and amanecerse (to stay up until morning).
variants.es: Spain says volver instead of regresar(se) (vuelvo a casa = I am going back home), and tardar has no se (tardo diez minutos = I will take ten minutes).

rules.title: Conjugation
rules.text: levantarse: me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos, se levantan.

rules.title: Where the pronoun goes
rules.text: Before the conjugated verb. With an infinitive or a gerund it can also be attached to the end.
examples: I'm going to take a shower.
I'm going to take a shower.

rules.title: Negation
rules.text: No goes before the pronoun.

rules.title: Not something English shows
rules.text: English almost never marks these verbs, so each one has to be learned: some need the pronoun, and some that feel as if they should don't.

title: Accents that change the meaning
intro: The mark over a vowel (á, é, í, ó, ú) shows the stress. In some words it is the only difference between two words, which is why the app doesn't let it pass there.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere.
variants.es: Accents are written the same in Spain. The pronunciation differs: in most of Spain z, and c before e and i, sound like English th (gracias, cerveza, cinco).

rules.title: Short words
rules.text: el = the, él = he. tu = your, tú = you. mi = my, mí = me. si = if, sí = yes. te = you (object), té = tea. se = himself / herself, sé = I know. mas = but, más = more.

rules.title: Question words
rules.text: In a question they carry an accent: qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, quién, cuánto. Without it they are linking words.

rules.title: Verb forms
rules.text: The accent changes the person and the tense: hablo = I speak, habló = he spoke. esta = this, está = is.

rules.title: Nouns
rules.text: papa = potato, papá = dad. The ñ can't always be dropped either: año = year.

title: The imperative
intro: Requests, advice and instructions: ven, siéntate, no te preocupes. The tú form is simple; the other persons take the subjunctive.

variants.mx: Mexico does not use vosotros: an order to several people takes the ustedes form (vengan, siéntense), among friends too. The voseo command (hablá, comé) is heard only in some southern states, for example Chiapas.
variants.es: In Spain an order to several people you would call tú takes the vosotros form: the -r of the infinitive becomes -d (hablad, comed, venid). Before os the -d drops: sentaos. Ustedes (vengan, siéntense) is the polite form.

rules.title: When it is used
rules.text: When you ask someone to do something, give advice or directions: a recipe, the way somewhere, an offer. With por favor it sounds polite.
examples: Go straight ahead and turn right.
Come in, make yourself at home.

rules.title: For tú: the él form
rules.text: The affirmative tú imperative is the present él form: habla, come, escribe, piensa, duerme.

rules.title: Short tú forms
rules.text: ven (venir), di (decir), sal (salir), haz (hacer), ten (tener), ve (ir), pon (poner), sé (ser). Compounds get an accent: mantén, propón, prevén.

rules.title: For usted, nosotros and ustedes: the subjunctive
rules.text: hable, hablemos, hablen; tenga, tengamos, tengan; vaya, vayan (for nosotros people mostly say vamos).

rules.title: Negative imperative: no + subjunctive
rules.text: The same for every person: no hables, no vengas, no hagas eso, no se preocupe.
examples: Don't make noise, the baby is asleep.

rules.title: Pronouns
rules.text: With an affirmative imperative the pronoun goes on the end. The stress stays on the same syllable, so it is written: siéntate, levántense, dímelo. With a negative one it goes before the verb: no te sientes, no me lo digas.

title: Present subjunctive: forms
intro: The subjunctive is the mood for what someone wants or feels, or what is not certain. It is built from the present with the “opposite” vowel: -ar verbs take endings with -e, -er and -ir verbs endings with -a.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere. The vosotros form: habléis, comáis, tengáis.

rules.title: When it is used
rules.text: After verbs of wishing and feeling when the second clause has another subject (quiero que vengas), after ojalá, after para que and with a negative opinion (no creo que).
examples: I'm calling so you know the news.

rules.title: -ar verbs: endings with -e
rules.text: hablar: hable, hables, hable, hablemos, hablen.
examples: I hope you talk to her.

rules.title: -er and -ir verbs: endings with -a
rules.text: comer: coma, comas, coma, comamos, coman. vivir: viva, vivas, viva, vivamos, vivan.
examples: I want you to eat something.

rules.title: The stem of the yo form
rules.text: Take the present yo form, drop -o and add the ending: tengo → tenga, hago → haga, conozco → conozca, salgo → salga, digo → diga. The stem stays in every person: tengamos, hagamos.
examples: It's better if we do it today.

rules.title: Stem change
rules.text: The stem changes as in the present: pueda, quiera, duerma, pida. In the nosotros form -ar and -er verbs keep their stem (podamos, queramos); -ir verbs change e to i and o to u (sintamos, durmamos, pidamos).
examples: I don't think she can come.
It's important that we sleep well.

rules.title: Spelling change
rules.text: Verbs in -car, -gar, -zar change their spelling before -e to keep their sound: buscar → busque, llegar → llegue, empezar → empiece.
examples: Let me know when you get there.

rules.title: Irregular verbs
rules.text: ser: sea · ir: vaya · estar: esté · saber: sepa · dar: dé · haber: haya.

title: The conditional (would)
intro: It says what would happen or what you would do. It is also the polite way to ask for something.

variants.mx: In Mexico the conditional is used a lot to be polite, often together with usted (¿me podría ayudar?). In reported speech Mexico prefers iba a + infinitive: Me dijo que iba a venir (instead of vendría).
variants.es: Spain too uses the conditional to be polite (¿me podría ayudar?, me gustaría un café). In a shop or a café people often use the imperfecto as well: quería un café = I would like a coffee.

rules.title: Infinitive + -ía
rules.text: hablar: hablaría, hablarías, hablaría, hablaríamos, hablarían. Likewise comería, viviría.
examples: I would talk to the boss.

rules.title: The same stem as the future
rules.text: tener → tendría, poder → podría, salir → saldría, venir → vendría, poner → pondría, decir → diría, hacer → haría, querer → querría, saber → sabría, haber → habría.
examples: We could go to the movies.

rules.title: A polite request
rules.text: Me gustaría, ¿podría…?, ¿te importaría…? sound more polite than the present.
examples: Could you help me with this?

rules.title: Advice and imagining
rules.text: Yo que tú… means “if I were you”. The unreal condition (if I had…) is in the tip on the imperfect subjunctive.
examples: If I were you, I'd take the bus.

variants.mx: In Mexico he hablado is used less: for today and the recent past people say the pretérito (hoy comí tacos, ya terminé). The perfecto is heard rather for experience and for what lasts until now (¿has ido a Oaxaca?, he vivido aquí diez años).
variants.es: In Spain it is the everyday past tense for today and for a period that is not over (hoy he comido paella, esta semana he trabajado mucho), also with ya and todavía no (ya he terminado). The pretérito stays for yesterday and earlier (ayer comí paella).

title: Present perfect (he hablado)
intro: An action in a period that is not over yet (today, this week) or that matters now: hoy he comido tacos. In Spain it is an everyday past tense; in Mexico it is used less.

rules.title: When it is used
rules.text: In Spain for an action in a period that is not over: hoy, esta semana, este año, and with ya, todavía no, alguna vez. For yesterday and earlier it takes the preterite: ayer comí. In Mexico the preterite is normal in all these cases.
rules.because: The period is not over (hoy, esta semana, ya…), so he + participle.
examples: This week I have worked a lot.

rules.title: he + participle
rules.text: haber in the present (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han) and the participle, which does not change: hablar → hablado, comer → comido, vivir → vivido. After a vowel -ído: leído, traído.
rules.because: The perfect is haber in the present (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han) and a participle in -ado / -ido.
examples: Have you already seen the movie?

rules.title: Irregular participles
rules.text: hacer → hecho, decir → dicho, ver → visto, escribir → escrito, poner → puesto, volver → vuelto, abrir → abierto, romper → roto, morir → muerto, resolver → resuelto.
rules.because: This verb has an irregular participle.

rules.title: Ayer, el año pasado: preterite
rules.text: When the period is over (ayer, anoche, la semana pasada, el año pasado, en 2020), Spain says the preterite too: ayer comí paella, but hoy he comido pescado.
rules.because: The period is over (ayer, la semana pasada…), so the preterite, not he + participle.
examples: Last night we watched a film.
This morning I saw your brother.

title: Pluperfect (had done)
intro: An action that happened before another past action: when I arrived, the movie had already started.

variants.mx: The pluscuamperfecto is the same as elsewhere. Mexico uses he comido less, see the rule on the pretérito perfecto.
variants.es: The pluscuamperfecto is the same as elsewhere; the vosotros form: habíais comido. He comido is Spain’s usual tense for today, see the rule on the pretérito perfecto.

rules.title: When it is used
rules.text: When you talk about the past and need to say what happened even earlier. Often with ya (already) and nunca (never).
examples: When I arrived, the movie had already started.

rules.title: había + participle
rules.text: haber in the imperfect (había, habías, había, habíamos, habían) and the participle, which does not change: hablar → hablado, comer → comido, vivir → vivido. After a vowel -ído: leído, traído.
examples: I had never seen the sea.

rules.title: Irregular participles
rules.text: hacer → hecho, decir → dicho, ver → visto, escribir → escrito, poner → puesto, volver → vuelto, abrir → abierto, romper → roto, morir → muerto, resolver → resuelto.
examples: I told him I had already done it.

rules.title: What about he comido?
rules.text: The present perfect (he comido, has ido) exists in Mexico too, but mostly for “ever” and “not yet”. A finished action, even today’s, takes the preterite: Hoy comí tacos.
examples: Have you ever been to Oaxaca?

title: Imperfect subjunctive: forms
intro: The past subjunctive. You need it in an unreal condition (si tuviera…) and in a second clause when the main clause is in the past (quería que vinieras).

variants.mx: Mexico uses the -ra form (hablara, tuviera); the -se form (hablase) is hardly heard there.
variants.es: Spain uses both the -ra form (hablara, tuviera) and the -se form (hablase, tuviese); they mean the same. Forming the -ra one is enough, the -se one needs recognizing.

rules.title: When it is used
rules.text: In an unreal condition (si + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional), in a wish that will probably not come true (ojalá pudiera), and in a second clause after a past tense (quería que, me pidió que).
examples: My parents wanted me to study medicine.
If I were you, I wouldn't tell him anything.

rules.title: From the preterite ellos form
rules.text: Take the preterite ellos form and change -ron to -ra: hablaron → hablara, tuvieron → tuviera, fueron → fuera, pidieron → pidiera. So the preterite’s irregularities carry over. The nosotros form gets an accent: habláramos, tuviéramos.
examples: If I had more time, I would travel more.
She asked me to go with her.

rules.title: The -se form
rules.text: Spain also uses hablase, tuviese. In Mexico you hardly hear it, so there is no need to learn it.
examples: I wish I could help you.

title: gustar, encantar, doler
intro: Me gusta does not mean “I like” but “it pleases me”: the thing liked is the subject. So the verb agrees with the thing, not the person.

variants.mx: In everyday Mexican speech you also hear me late (= I have a hunch: me late que va a llover; also = I like it: me late tu carro), but gustar is always right.
variants.es: In everyday speech Spain also says me mola (= I like it, it is cool: me mola tu coche) or me flipa, but gustar is always right.

rules.title: The thing liked is the subject
rules.text: Me gusta el café = I like coffee (coffee pleases me). Before an infinitive it is always gusta: me gusta bailar.
rules.because: What is liked is the subject, so gustar agrees with it.

rules.title: Several things: gustan
rules.text: When several things are liked, the verb is plural: me gustan los tacos.
rules.because: More than one thing is liked, so gustan.

rules.title: Who likes it
rules.text: me, te, le, nos, les. For emphasis or clarity add a mí, a ti, a ella, a mis papás.
rules.because: Who likes it is said by me, te, le, nos, les.

rules.title: Likewise encantar, doler, interesar
rules.text: me encanta (I love it), me duele (it hurts), me interesa, me importa, me molesta.
rules.because: This verb works like gustar: it agrees with the thing, not the person.

title: hay or estar
intro: Hay says that something exists or is available somewhere. Estar says where a specific, known thing is.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere. In Latin America you sometimes hear habían cajas or hubieron cajas; the correct forms are hay, había, hubo cajas, always singular.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere.

rules.title: Hay: there is
rules.text: Hay never changes. Before the thing comes un, una, a number or nothing: hay un Oxxo, hay dos camiones, no hay leche.
rules.because: It says that something is there (un, una, a number or nothing), so hay.
examples: There's an Oxxo on the corner.
There's no milk in the fridge.

rules.title: Estar: where the known thing is
rules.text: Before the thing comes el, la, mi, tu or a name: el Oxxo está, mi celular está, Ana está.
rules.because: It says where a known thing is (el, la, mi, a name), so estar.
examples: The Oxxo is on the corner.

rules.title: In a question
rules.text: ¿Hay un banco por aquí? = is there a bank around here? ¿Dónde está el banco? = where is the bank?
rules.because: In a question too: whether something is there → hay, where a known thing is → estar.
examples: Is there a pharmacy around here?

title: Object pronouns (lo, la, le)
intro: Instead of repeating the noun: ¿El pastel? Lo compré. Lo and la are for whom or what, le for to whom.

variants.mx: When the person is the direct object, Mexico says lo/la (lo vi ayer = I saw him); le vi sounds like Spain. Le for “to whom” (le doy) and the polite le with usted (¿le ayudo?) are common. Mexico also adds le for emphasis (¡Ándale! = come on; ¿Qué le haces? = what are you doing?). “We had a good time” is la pasamos bien (Spain: lo pasamos bien).
variants.es: When the direct object is a man, Spain often says le instead of lo (le vi ayer = I saw him), mostly in the centre and the north. It is accepted as correct. For things it stays lo (¿el libro? lo tengo).

rules.title: lo, la, los, las: whom, what
rules.text: They follow the gender and number of the thing: el libro → lo, la casa → la, los boletos → los, las llaves → las.
rules.because: The pronoun stands for the thing or person (whom, what) and agrees with it.
examples: The cake? I bought it yesterday.
Do you have the keys? Yes, I have them.

rules.title: le, les: to whom
rules.text: Le for one person (usted too), les for several. The person is often named as well: le di el libro a Ana.
rules.because: It is about to whom: le for one, les for more.
examples: Did you write to your parents?

rules.title: Where they go
rules.text: Before a conjugated verb: lo compro. Attached to an infinitive, a gerund and an affirmative imperative: voy a comprarlo, estoy haciéndolo, cómpralo.
rules.because: The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb or joins the infinitive, gerund or imperative.

rules.title: Two pronouns: se lo
rules.text: First to whom, then what. Le and les become se before lo, la: le doy el libro → se lo doy. This is B1.
rules.because: Two pronouns: le, les turns into se before lo, la.
examples: The present? I gave it to Marta.

title: Comparing
intro: More, less, as much, the most: más alto que, tan caro como, el mejor.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere.

rules.title: más / menos … que
rules.text: Más barato que, menos caro que. Before a number de: más de cien pesos.
rules.because: More or less is compared: más / menos … que.
examples: My brother is taller than me.
The bus is cheaper than a taxi.

rules.title: tan … como, tanto … como
rules.text: With an adjective tan: tan caro como. With a noun tanto, tanta, tantos, tantas: tantos libros como tú.
rules.because: Sameness is compared: tan … como (tanto before a noun).
examples: This phone is as good as the other one.
I don't have as much time as you.

rules.title: mejor, peor, mayor, menor
rules.text: bueno → mejor, malo → peor. For age mayor (older) and menor (younger). Nobody says más bueno.
rules.because: Bueno and malo have forms of their own: mejor, peor (age: mayor, menor).
examples: This salsa is better than the other one.
My younger sister lives in Puebla.

rules.title: The most: el más, -ísimo
rules.text: el / la más … de: la más alta de la clase. Very: -ísimo (carísimo, riquísimo).
rules.because: It is the most: el / la más … de, or -ísimo.
examples: It's the most famous restaurant in the city.

title: Have to, should, can
intro: tener que, hay que, deber and poder go with an infinitive: tengo que trabajar.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere, most often with tener que (tengo que trabajar).
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere, most often with tener que (tengo que trabajar).

rules.title: tener que: I have to
rules.text: An obligation of a particular person. Tener is conjugated, the infinitive does not change.
rules.because: A particular person has to, so tener que.
examples: I have to work on Saturday.
We had to wait an hour.

rules.title: hay que: one has to
rules.text: No person: it applies to everyone.
rules.because: It has to be done in general, with no person, so hay que.
examples: You have to pay in cash.

rules.title: deber: I should
rules.text: Advice or duty. Debería (conditional) sounds softer.
rules.because: It is advice or a duty (should), so deber.

rules.title: poder: I can
rules.text: Ability and permission. Politely podría, podrías.
rules.because: It is ability or permission, so poder.

title: The subjunctive for wishes and feelings
intro: When someone wants, hopes or feels something about another person, the que clause is in the subjunctive: quiero que vengas.

variants.mx: Ojalá is very common in everyday Mexican conversation (ojalá que llueva).
variants.es: Ojalá is common in Spain too, with or without que (ojalá llueva, ojalá que apruebes = I hope you pass the exam).

rules.title: Wanting: quiero que
rules.text: Two different subjects → que + subjunctive (quiero que vengas). The same subject → infinitive (quiero venir).
rules.because: Someone wants someone else to do something: que + subjunctive.
examples: I want you to come to the party.
I want to go to the party.

rules.title: Feelings: me alegra que, espero que
rules.text: me alegra que, me molesta que, me preocupa que, espero que, tengo miedo de que.
rules.because: After a feeling (me alegra, espero, me preocupa) comes que + subjunctive.

rules.title: Advice and need
rules.text: te recomiendo que, te pido que, es importante que, es mejor que, es necesario que.
rules.because: After advice or need (es importante, te recomiendo) comes que + subjunctive.
examples: I recommend you try the mole.
It's important that you arrive on time.

rules.title: Ojalá
rules.text: Ojalá (let’s hope) always takes the subjunctive.
rules.because: Ojalá is always followed by the subjunctive.
examples: Let's hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.

title: Conditions with si
intro: Si means “if”. Which tense follows depends on whether the condition is real or only imagined.

variants.mx: In Mexico an if-clause takes the -ra form (si tuviera tiempo…); the -se form (si tuviese) is hardly heard.
variants.es: In Spain an if-clause takes the -ra or the -se form (si tuviera tiempo… / si tuviese tiempo…); both are right.

rules.title: Real: si + present
rules.text: Si llueve, me quedo en casa. The second part can be in the present, the future or the imperative.
rules.because: The condition can be true: si + present.
examples: If it rains, I stay home.
If you have time, call me.

rules.title: Unreal: si + imperfect subjunctive
rules.text: Something imagined that is not true now: si tuviera dinero, compraría un carro. The conditional follows. This is B2.
rules.because: The condition is not true now: si + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional.
examples: If I had money, I would buy a car.
If we lived closer, we would see each other more.

rules.title: What never follows si
rules.text: No future, conditional or present subjunctive after si. Not si vendrás, but si vienes.
rules.because: After si there is no future or conditional, but the present.
examples: If you come tomorrow, I'll show you the photos.

title: por or para
intro: Both often mean “for”. Para looks ahead, to a goal. Por looks at the cause, the way and the exchange.

variants.mx: In everyday Mexican speech para is often shortened to pa’ (pa’ que sepas); in writing it is spelled out.
variants.es: In everyday speech Spain too shortens para to pa’ (me voy pa’ casa); in writing it is spelled out.

rules.title: para: the goal
rules.text: Purpose (para aprender), recipient (para ti), deadline (para el lunes), direction (salgo para Monterrey), opinion (para mí).
rules.because: It is a goal: a purpose, for whom, a deadline or a direction, so para.
examples: I need the report by Monday.

rules.title: por: cause and way
rules.text: Cause (por el tráfico), through (por el parque), exchange and price (por cien pesos), means (por teléfono), part of the day (por la mañana).
rules.because: It is a cause, a way through, an exchange or a means, so por.
examples: I was late because of the traffic.
I bought it for a hundred pesos.

rules.title: Set phrases
rules.text: por favor, por fin, por ejemplo, por eso, por supuesto; para nada, para siempre.
rules.because: It is a set phrase, learnt as a whole.
examples: Does it bother you? Not at all.

title: The subjunctive after opinions and conjunctions
intro: The subjunctive follows a negative opinion, doubt and the conjunctions cuando, antes de que and para que, when something is not certain yet.

variants.mx: In Mexico you often hear capaz que + subjunctive for “maybe” (capaz que llueva = it may rain).
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere.

rules.title: Opinion: creo que, no creo que
rules.text: creo que, pienso que, me parece que + indicative. Their negative (no creo que) and doubt (dudo que, es posible que, puede que) + subjunctive.
rules.because: A denied opinion or doubt (no creo que, dudo que) takes the subjunctive, an opinion (creo que) does not.

rules.title: cuando about the future
rules.text: cuando, antes de que, después de que + subjunctive about the future (cuando llegues, antes de que llueva). Cuando about a habit or the past takes the indicative (cuando llego, cuando llegué).
rules.because: Cuando about the future takes the subjunctive, about habits or the past it does not.
examples: When you get there, let me know.
When I get home, I take a shower.

rules.title: para que: so that
rules.text: para que always takes the subjunctive. With the same subject para + infinitive is enough.
rules.because: Para que (so that) always takes the subjunctive.
examples: I'll explain it so you understand it.
I'm saving to buy a house.

title: The subjunctive after aunque and hasta que
intro: With aunque it depends on whether it is a fact or something possible that does not matter. The time conjunctions hasta que, en cuanto and una vez que take the subjunctive about the future.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere.

rules.title: aunque: although, even if
rules.text: aunque + indicative = it is so (aunque llueve, salgo). aunque + subjunctive = maybe, it does not matter (aunque llueva, salgo).
rules.because: Aunque + subjunctive: maybe, it does not matter; + indicative: it is so.
examples: Although he's tired, he keeps working.
Even if it rains, we'll go.

rules.title: a pesar de que: despite the fact that
rules.text: Like aunque: with the indicative it is a fact (a pesar de que llueve), with the subjunctive it is possible or does not matter (a pesar de que llueva). Before a noun without que: a pesar del frío.
rules.because: A pesar de que works like aunque: a fact takes the indicative, something possible or unimportant the subjunctive.
examples: Although he was sick, he went to work.
I'm going to try it, even if it turns out to be hard.

rules.title: hasta que, en cuanto, una vez que
rules.text: About the future the subjunctive follows: espera hasta que llegue, en cuanto sepa algo, te aviso. About the past or a habit, the indicative: esperé hasta que llegó.
rules.because: Hasta que, en cuanto and una vez que about the future take the subjunctive.
examples: As soon as I know something, I will let you know.
I'll stay here until you finish.

title: Relative clauses (que, donde, lo que)
intro: They join two sentences into one: el libro que leí. Que is the most common and works for people and things.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere; in speech que is the most common, el cual sounds bookish.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere; in speech que is the most common, el cual sounds bookish.

rules.title: que: who, which, that
rules.text: For people and things, without a preposition: la señora que vive arriba, el libro que me prestaste.
rules.because: Without a preposition, people and things take que.
examples: The lady who lives upstairs is very kind.
Have you read the book I lent you yet?

rules.title: donde: where
rules.text: A place: la casa donde vivo, el pueblo donde nací.
rules.because: It is a place, so donde.
examples: This is the market where I buy fruit.

rules.title: lo que: what
rules.text: When it is not a particular thing: lo que dices, todo lo que quieras.
rules.because: It is not a particular thing but "what", so lo que.
examples: I don't understand what you're saying.

title: Relative clauses after a preposition (con la que, quien, cuyo)
intro: When the relative word follows a preposition, an article is added: la persona con la que hablé. For people quien works too, and cuyo says whom something belongs to.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere; cuyo belongs rather to written and formal language.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere; cuyo belongs rather to written and formal language.

rules.title: After a preposition: el que, la que, quien
rules.text: After a preposition the article is added: la persona con la que hablé, el tema del que te hablé. For people also quien: la chava con quien salgo.
rules.because: After a preposition the article comes in: el que, la que (for people also quien).
examples: That's the girl I work with.
It's the topic I told you about.

rules.title: quien, quienes: who (people)
rules.text: Only for people, when the clause sits between commas: mi hermano, quien vive en Puebla. Que works too. Without a comma and without a preposition only que.
rules.because: It is a person in a clause between commas, so quien (que works too).
examples: My brother, who lives in Puebla, is coming tomorrow.

rules.title: cuyo, cuya: whose
rules.text: Says whom something belongs to: la vecina cuyo perro ladra (the neighbour whose dog barks). It agrees with what is owned, not with the owner. Sounds rather bookish.
rules.because: It says whom something belongs to, so cuyo; it agrees with what is owned.
examples: I have a friend whose sister lives in Mérida.

title: Impersonal and passive se
intro: When who does it does not matter, se is used: se vende, aquí se habla español. It is common in speech as well as on signs and in ads.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere; typical on signs and in ads (se vende, se renta = for rent).
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere; typical on signs and in ads (se vende, se alquila = for rent).

rules.title: se + verb
rules.text: se vende, se rentan departamentos, aquí se habla español. The verb agrees with the thing: se vende casa, se venden casas.
rules.because: Se + verb: an action with no doer, the verb agrees with the thing.

rules.title: Impersonal se
rules.text: With no thing, about people in general: ¿cómo se dice…?, aquí se vive bien.
rules.because: Impersonal se: it speaks about people in general.
examples: How do you say this in Spanish?

rules.title: estar + participle: a state
rules.text: Estar with a participle does not describe an action but its result: la tienda está cerrada.
rules.because: Estar + participle describes the state after the action, not the action.

title: The passive with ser (fue construido)
intro: The passive with ser tells an action from the side of what it happens to: el puente fue construido. It belongs to the news, textbooks and official texts.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere: in the news and official texts; speech prefers se or the active.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere: in the news and official texts; speech prefers se or the active.

rules.title: ser + participle
rules.text: ser + participle: el puente fue construido en 1990. The participle agrees with the subject (la casa fue vendida, los libros fueron publicados). Who did it is added with por: fue escrito por Octavio Paz.
rules.because: The passive: ser + a participle that agrees with the subject.

rules.title: Where it is used
rules.text: In the news, in textbooks and in official texts. In everyday speech the same is said with se or in the active: se construyó el puente, construyeron el puente.
rules.because: The passive with ser belongs to the news and official texts; speech would use se or the active.
examples: The results will be announced on Monday.
The museum was opened by the president.

title: este, ese, aquel
intro: Demonstratives have three degrees of distance: este (this, by me), ese (that, by you), aquel (that over there, far from us both). They change for gender and number like adjectives.

variants.mx: In Mexico ese is by far the most common in speech; aquel is for something really far away or long ago (en aquel entonces = back then). Instead of aquí and allí, Mexicans more often say acá and allá: ven acá.
variants.es: In Spain aquí and allí are more common than acá and allá; este, ese and aquel work as in Mexico.

rules.title: este: by me
rules.text: este libro, esta mesa, estos zapatos, estas llaves. It goes before the noun, without an article (not el este libro).
rules.because: The thing is close to the speaker, so este (esta, estos, estas).

rules.title: ese, aquel: further away
rules.text: ese (esa, esos, esas) is by you or a bit further, aquel (aquella, aquellos, aquellas) far from both of you. In everyday speech ese is usually enough.
rules.because: The thing is further from the speaker, so ese or aquel.
examples: Can you pass me that cup?
Do you see that mountain over there?

rules.title: esto, eso: an unknown thing or an idea
rules.text: When you don’t know what something is, or you mean a whole situation, use esto, eso, aquello. They have no plural and never stand before a noun.
rules.because: It is an unknown thing or a whole idea, so esto or eso.

rules.title: With time: esta tarde, aquel año
rules.text: With time, este points to now (esta tarde = this afternoon, este fin de semana), ese and aquel to the past (aquel verano = that summer).
rules.because: It is about time: este is now, ese and aquel the past.
examples: This afternoon I’m going to the movies.
That summer we went to the beach.

rules.title: Without a noun: este no, ese sí
rules.text: A demonstrative can stand alone when it is clear what it refers to. Under today’s rules it has no written accent (este, not éste).
rules.because: The noun is clear from the context, so the demonstrative stands alone.
examples: I don’t like that one, I prefer this one.
Which one do you want? —That one.

title: mi, tu, su… mío, tuyo
intro: A possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. Before a noun it is the short form (mi, tu, su), after ser the long one (mío, tuyo, suyo).

variants.mx: In Mexico people often say la casa de nosotros instead of nuestra casa. Su also means your for several people (ustedes), since vosotros is not used.
variants.es: In Spain vuestro is used for several people you address informally (vuestra casa, vuestros hijos); su for ustedes is only formal there.

rules.title: mi, tu, su: only number changes
rules.text: mi casa, mis amigos; tu carro, tus llaves. Gender does not change: mi hermano and mi hermana. Careful: tu (your) has no accent, tú (you) has one.
rules.because: Before a noun comes the short form mi, tu, su; for several things mis, tus, sus.

rules.title: nuestro, nuestra: gender too
rules.text: nuestro departamento, nuestra casa, nuestros hijos, nuestras amigas. It agrees with the thing, not with its owners.
rules.because: nuestro agrees with the thing in gender and number.

rules.title: su: his, her, your, their
rules.text: su means his, her, their and also your (formal: usted, ustedes). When it is unclear whose, say de él, de ella, de ellos: la casa de ella.
rules.because: The owner is he, she, usted or they, so su (sus).
examples: Ana and her boyfriend live together.

rules.title: Slovak “svoj”
rules.text: Spanish has no word like Slovak svoj (one’s own): the possessive follows the person. I have my umbrella = tengo mi paraguas, you have yours = tienes tu paraguas, each has their own = cada uno tiene su paraguas.
rules.because: Slovak svoj is translated by the person: mi, tu, su, nuestro.
examples: I left my umbrella on the bus.

rules.title: mío, tuyo: after ser and alone
rules.text: After ser or after a noun comes the long form: es mío, un amigo mío. With an article it replaces the whole noun: el mío, la tuya.
rules.because: After ser or without a noun comes the long form mío, tuyo, suyo.
examples: Your car is red and mine is blue.

rules.title: Body and clothes: the article is enough
rules.text: With body parts and clothes Spanish usually uses the article, not a possessive: me duele la cabeza, me lavo las manos.
rules.because: With a body part it is clear whose it is, so the article is enough.
examples: Put your jacket on, it’s cold.

title: Questions: qué, quién, dónde…
intro: Question words come first in a question and always carry a written accent: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto, cuál. A question opens with an upside-down question mark ¿.

variants.mx: In Mexico, when you didn’t catch something or someone calls you, you say ¿Mande? (pardon?), not ¿Qué?, which can sound rude. Also common: ¿Qué tanto? (how much) and ¿A poco? (really?).
variants.es: In Spain instead of ¿Mande? people say ¿Perdona? or ¿Cómo?; instead of ¿Qué tanto? they say ¿Cuánto?

rules.title: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cómo, cuánto
rules.text: qué (what), quién (who, for several quiénes), dónde (where), cuándo (when), cómo (how), cuánto (how much / many). Cuánto agrees with the noun: cuántos años, cuántas hermanas.
rules.because: You ask about a thing, a person, a place, a time, a manner or an amount, so this question word.
examples: How many sisters do you have?

rules.title: The preposition comes first
rules.text: The preposition stands before the question word, never at the end: ¿De dónde eres? (where are you from), ¿Con quién vives?, ¿A qué hora empieza?, ¿Para qué sirve?
rules.because: The preposition belongs before the question word, at the start of the question.
examples: What time does the bus leave?

rules.title: ¿Por qué? and porque
rules.text: In a question it is two words and qué has an accent: ¿por qué? (why). In an answer it is one word without an accent: porque (because).
rules.because: In a question it is por qué, in an answer porque.
examples: I didn’t come because I was sick.

rules.title: ¿Qué? or ¿cuál?
rules.text: Before a noun it is qué: ¿Qué libro lees? Before es and when choosing among options it is cuál: ¿Cuál es tu número?, ¿Cuál prefieres? ¿Qué es…? asks what something is: ¿Qué es un tamal?
rules.because: You ask for one of several options or for a piece of data (name, number, address), so cuál.
examples: What movie do you want to see?

title: Negation: no, nunca, nada, nadie
intro: No before the verb makes a sentence negative. Nunca, nada, nadie, tampoco and ningún mean never, nothing, nobody, neither and no (none). Unlike in English, a double negative is required, but only when they come after the verb.

variants.mx: In Mexico you often hear ni modo (oh well, nothing to be done) and para nada (not at all). In some Latin American countries también no is heard instead of tampoco, but tampoco is correct. Colloquially you also hear más nada, más nadie (ya no hay más nada = there is nothing else) and hasta without no: Llega hasta mañana = he arrives only tomorrow.
variants.es: In Spain instead of ni modo people rather say qué le vamos a hacer; para nada is common there too.

rules.title: no before the verb
rules.text: no comes right before the verb. When the verb has a pronoun (lo, me, se), no goes before the pronoun: No lo sé.
rules.because: No goes before the verb and before its pronouns.

rules.title: nadie, nada, nunca: where they stand
rules.text: After the verb you also need no: No veo a nadie (I don’t see anybody). When they come before the verb, no is left out: Nadie vino, Nunca como carne.
rules.because: The negative word comes after the verb, so no as well; before the verb there would be no no.

rules.title: también and tampoco
rules.text: también = too, tampoco = neither. To agree with a negative sentence say tampoco: —No tengo hambre. —Yo tampoco. With gustar: a mí también, a mí tampoco.
rules.because: You agree with a negative sentence, so tampoco (with a positive one también).
examples: My brother doesn’t speak English either.

rules.title: algo – nada, alguien – nadie, algún – ningún
rules.text: A positive word has a negative partner: algo (something) – nada (nothing), alguien (somebody) – nadie (nobody), algún (some) – ningún (no, none). Ningún is singular only: no tengo ningún problema.
rules.because: In a negative sentence the negative partner is used: nada, nadie, ningún.
examples: Do you want anything? —No, nothing, thanks.

title: Personal a
intro: When the object of a verb is a specific person, Spanish puts a before it: Veo a María. Not before things: Veo la tele. This a is not translated.

variants.mx: In Mexico the same as in Spain. Common verbs with a person: extrañar a alguien (to miss someone), invitar a alguien, llevar a alguien.
variants.es: The same in Spain; instead of extrañar people say echar de menos a alguien.

rules.title: A person: a
rules.text: When you see, know, call, look for or wait for someone, a goes before the person (a + el = al). It also goes before a pet you are close to.
rules.because: The object of the verb is a person, so a goes before it.

rules.title: A thing: no a
rules.text: Before things and places there is no a: veo la tele, busco un departamento, visito la ciudad.
rules.because: The object is a thing, so no a.
examples: I’m looking for an apartment near downtown.

rules.title: tener and hay: no a
rules.text: After tener and hay there is no a, even before a person: Tengo dos hermanos, Hay mucha gente.
rules.because: After tener and hay there is no a, even before a person.
examples: I have three cousins in Guadalajara.
There’s a man at the door.

rules.title: a quién, a alguien, a nadie
rules.text: a also goes before quién, alguien and nadie when they are the object: ¿A quién buscas?, ¿Conoces a alguien aquí?, No conozco a nadie.
rules.because: Quién, alguien and nadie stand for a person, so a goes before them.
examples: I don’t know anybody in this city.

title: Verb phrases: acabar de, volver a, soler…
intro: A verb phrase is a pair of verbs: the first is conjugated, the second is an infinitive or a gerund. It tells you what stage the action is in: just finished, starting, repeated, habitual, stopping or still going.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere. In casual speech soler is often replaced by normalmente or generalmente (normalmente desayuno a las siete).
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere.

rules.title: acabar de: I just did it
rules.text: Acabar de + infinitive means the action has just ended: Acabo de llegar. Acabar is in the present tense even though the action is in the past.
rules.because: The action has just ended, so acabar de + infinitive.
examples: I have just arrived at the office.

rules.title: empezar a, ponerse a: to start
rules.text: Empezar a or ponerse a + infinitive means to start doing something. The a is required.
rules.because: It is about the start of the action, so empezar a / ponerse a + infinitive.
examples: I started studying Spanish last year.

rules.title: volver a: to do it again
rules.text: Volver a + infinitive means to do something again. English uses “again”, Spanish uses the verb volver.
rules.because: The action is repeated, so volver a + infinitive.
examples: Tomorrow I will call you again.

rules.title: soler: to usually do
rules.text: Soler + infinitive means you usually do something. It is used almost only in the present and the imperfect.
rules.because: It is a habit, so soler + infinitive.
examples: I usually have breakfast at seven.
As a child I used to play in the street.

rules.title: dejar de: to stop
rules.text: Dejar de + infinitive means to stop doing something: Dejé de fumar.
rules.because: The action is stopping, so dejar de + infinitive.
examples: I stopped smoking two years ago.

rules.title: seguir + gerund: still doing
rules.text: Seguir + gerund means the action is still going on: Sigo trabajando en el mismo lugar.
rules.because: The action is still going on, so seguir + gerund.
examples: I still work in the same place.
My parents still live in Puebla.

title: Time clauses: cuando, mientras, antes de que
intro: Time clauses say when something happens. The word that opens them decides the verb form: indicative for the past and habits, subjunctive for the future.

variants.mx: In Mexico hasta without no is also used for a start: Llega hasta mañana = he arrives only tomorrow.
variants.es: In Spain that meaning is No llega hasta mañana.

rules.title: antes de, después de + infinitive
rules.text: When both verbs have the same subject, antes de or después de + infinitive is used: Antes de salir, apago la luz.
rules.because: The subject is the same, so antes de / después de + infinitive.
examples: Before leaving, I turn off all the lights.
After eating, I have a coffee.

rules.title: cuando: indicative or subjunctive
rules.text: For the past and habits cuando takes the indicative (Cuando llegué, llovía). For the future it takes the subjunctive (Cuando llegues, llámame).
rules.because: It is about a future that has not happened yet, so the subjunctive. The past and habits take the indicative.
examples: When I arrived, everyone was already there.

rules.title: mientras: two things at once
rules.text: Mientras + indicative means “while”, two actions run at the same time: Mientras cocino, escucho música.
rules.because: Two actions run at once, so mientras + indicative.
examples: While I cook, I listen to music.
While you were sleeping, I was working.

rules.title: antes de que + subjunctive
rules.text: When the subjects differ, antes de que + subjunctive is used: Llámame antes de que salgas.
rules.because: The subjects differ and the action has not happened, so antes de que + subjunctive.
examples: We will have dinner before the movie starts.

rules.title: desde, desde hace, hasta
rules.text: Desde is a point in time (desde 2020), desde hace is a duration (desde hace tres años), hasta is the end (hasta las seis).
rules.because: It is about a start, a duration or an end, so desde, desde hace or hasta.
examples: I have lived in Prague for three years.

title: Cause and result: como, así que, por eso
intro: You give a cause with porque, como or ya que, and a result with por eso, así que or entonces. The order of the clauses decides which one you use.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere. In casual speech es que often introduces a cause (Es que no tenía tiempo = It is just that I had no time).
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere; es que is used there too.

rules.title: porque and como: the cause
rules.text: If the cause comes after the main clause, use porque. If it comes before, use como: Llegué tarde porque había tráfico. Como había tráfico, llegué tarde.
rules.because: The cause clause comes before the main clause, so como. After it, it would be porque.
examples: I arrived late because there was traffic.
Since there was traffic, I arrived late.

rules.title: por eso, así que, entonces: the result
rules.text: A result is joined with por eso, así que or entonces: Hacía frío, así que me puse un suéter.
rules.because: It is about a result, so por eso, así que or entonces.
examples: I was tired, so I went to bed early.
It is cold, so I am wearing a sweater.

rules.title: ya que, puesto que: a cause you both know
rules.text: Ya que or puesto que gives a cause both people know: Ya que estás aquí, ayúdame. It sounds a bit formal.
rules.because: The cause is known to both, so ya que or puesto que.
examples: Since you are here, help me with this.
Since nobody answered, I hung up.

rules.title: tan… que, tanto… que: so… that
rules.text: Tan + adjective or adverb + que, tanto + verb + que: Estaba tan cansada que se durmió.
rules.because: The result comes from the degree of a quality, so tan… que or tanto… que.
examples: She was so tired that she fell asleep on the bus.
I ate so much that I cannot move.

title: Reported speech: dijo que…
intro: When you retell what someone said, the verb moves back in time after “dijo que”. Questions are carried by si or a question word, commands by que + subjunctive.

variants.mx: In Mexico the future after dijo que is most often iba a (Dijo que iba a venir). The conditional (vendría) is more formal.
variants.es: In Spain the conditional (dijo que vendría) is more common than in Mexico.

rules.title: dijo que: the tense moves back
rules.text: After dijo que the present becomes the imperfect and the pretérito becomes the pluscuamperfecto: “Tengo hambre” → Dijo que tenía hambre.
rules.because: It reports what someone said in the past, so the tense moves back.
examples: He told me he had arrived late.

rules.title: preguntó si, qué, dónde: an indirect question
rules.text: A yes/no question is carried by si, other questions keep their question word: Me preguntó si tenía tiempo.
rules.because: You are reporting a question, so si or the question word, and the tense moves back.
examples: He asked me if I had time.

rules.title: dijo que + subjunctive: a command
rules.text: When you report a command or advice, dijo que takes the subjunctive: Me dijo que tuviera cuidado.
rules.because: You are reporting a command or advice, so the subjunctive.
examples: He told me to be careful.
My mom says I should bundle up.

rules.title: The future in reported speech: iba a
rules.text: What was going to happen is most often said with iba a + infinitive in Mexico: Dijo que iba a venir. The conditional (vendría) is more formal.
rules.because: In speech the future in the past is said with iba a + infinitive.
examples: He told me he would come tomorrow.

title: Maybe: quizá, tal vez, a lo mejor, capaz que
intro: Spanish has several ways to say “maybe”. Some take the subjunctive, but a lo mejor always takes the indicative.

variants.mx: In Mexico capaz que is heard in casual speech (capaz que llueva = it may rain).
variants.es: Capaz que is not heard in Spain; people say quizá, tal vez or a lo mejor.

rules.title: quizá, tal vez + subjunctive
rules.text: After quizá, quizás and tal vez the subjunctive is used when you are not sure: Quizá venga mañana. If you are surer, the indicative is possible too.
rules.because: You are not sure, so quizá and tal vez take the subjunctive.

rules.title: a lo mejor + indicative
rules.text: A lo mejor means “maybe” and always takes the indicative, never the subjunctive: A lo mejor llego tarde.
rules.because: A lo mejor is always followed by the indicative.

rules.title: probablemente, seguramente: indicative or subjunctive
rules.text: After probablemente, seguramente and posiblemente the indicative (surer) is more common; the subjunctive (less sure) is mostly heard after probablemente and posiblemente: Probablemente está en casa.
rules.because: You are fairly sure, so the indicative. With more doubt it would be the subjunctive.
examples: It will probably rain this afternoon.

rules.title: capaz que + subjunctive
rules.text: Capaz que means “maybe” and takes the subjunctive. It is casual Mexican speech: Capaz que llueva.
rules.because: Capaz que means “maybe” and takes the subjunctive.
examples: Maybe it will rain in the afternoon.

title: Verbs with prepositions: pensar en, darse cuenta de
intro: Many verbs have a fixed preposition that you learn together with the verb. English or Slovak often uses a different one.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere. Watch out for casual dequeísmo (pienso de que…): the correct form is pienso que.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere.

rules.title: de: hablar de, acordarse de, darse cuenta de
rules.text: Verbs with de include hablar de, acordarse de, darse cuenta de, depender de.
rules.because: The verb goes with the preposition de.

rules.title: en: pensar en, confiar en, tardar en
rules.text: Verbs with en include pensar en, confiar en, tardar en, fijarse en.
rules.because: The verb goes with the preposition en.
examples: I am thinking about my vacation.
It took me an hour to get there.

rules.title: a: aprender a, ayudar a, empezar a
rules.text: Verbs with a include aprender a, ayudar a, empezar a, atreverse a.
rules.because: The verb goes with the preposition a.
examples: I learned to swim as a child.
He helped me move the armchair.

rules.title: con: contar con, soñar con, casarse con
rules.text: Verbs with con include contar con, soñar con, casarse con, encontrarse con.
rules.because: The verb goes with the preposition con.
examples: I am counting on you for tomorrow.
Last night I dreamed about my grandmother.

rules.title: The preposition changes the meaning
rules.text: With some verbs the preposition changes the meaning: pensar en = to think about, pensar de = to have an opinion on. Pienso en ti, ¿qué piensas de esto?
rules.because: The preposition belongs to the meaning, so en for “think about” and de for “have an opinion”.
examples: I think about you every day.
What do you think of my idea?

title: ser listo, estar listo: a change of meaning
intro: Some adjectives change meaning with the verb. With ser it is a trait, with estar a state or a result.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere. With estar a temporary state is often strengthened with bien (está bien cansado).
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere; it is strengthened with muy or súper (está súper cansado).

rules.title: listo, aburrido, malo, abierto
rules.text: Es listo = he is clever, está listo = he is ready. Es aburrido = he is boring, está aburrido = he is bored. Es malo = he is bad, está malo = he is sick.
rules.because: The verb changes the meaning: ser says a trait, estar a state.

rules.title: verde, seguro, rico, vivo
rules.text: Es verde = it is green, está verde = it is unripe. Es seguro = it is safe, estoy seguro = I am sure. Es rico = he is rich (for food also tasty), está rico = it is tasty right now.
rules.because: The verb changes the meaning: ser says a trait, estar a state.
examples: I am sure he is coming.

rules.title: es delgado, está delgado
rules.text: Es delgado = he is slim by nature. Está delgado = he has lost weight or looks thin now. The same goes for es guapo and está guapo.
rules.because: Estar says a change or a current impression, ser a trait.
examples: You are very thin, are you eating well?

title: Verbs of change: ponerse, quedarse, hacerse, volverse
intro: English “to become” has several Spanish verbs. They differ in whether the change is temporary, a result or the outcome of effort.

variants.mx: In Mexico ponerse is often strengthened with bien: se puso bien contento = he was really pleased.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere; instead of bien people say muy or súper.

rules.title: ponerse + adjective: a temporary change
rules.text: Ponerse + adjective expresses a temporary change, for example of mood, color or health: Se puso nervioso.
rules.because: The change is temporary, so ponerse.
examples: She got very nervous before the exam.

rules.title: quedarse + adjective: a result
rules.text: Quedarse + adjective or participle expresses a result, often an unpleasant one: Me quedé dormido.
rules.because: It is a result, so quedarse.
examples: I fell asleep on the bus.
He lost his job in March.

rules.title: hacerse + noun: the result of effort
rules.text: Hacerse + noun or adjective expresses a change someone achieved by effort or choice: hacerse médico, hacerse rico.
rules.because: The change comes from effort or choice, so hacerse.
examples: Over the years he became famous.

rules.title: volverse + adjective: a marked change
rules.text: Volverse + adjective expresses a marked, lasting change, sudden or gradual, often an unfavourable one: volverse loco, volverse desconfiado.
rules.because: The change is marked and lasting, so volverse.
examples: With the stress I am going crazy.

title: What would have been: habría ido, si hubiera sabido
intro: Things that did not happen in the past use haber + participle. Habría + participle is “would have”, hubiera + participle is “had”.

variants.mx: In Mexico casual speech puts hubiera in the main clause too (Si hubiera sabido, te hubiera llamado). In writing habría is kept.
variants.es: In Spain the main clause keeps habría (te habría llamado).

rules.title: habría + participle: what would have been
rules.text: Habría + participle expresses what would have happened but did not: Yo habría ido.
rules.because: It is about something that did not happen in the past, so habría + participle.
examples: I would have gone, but they did not invite me.

rules.title: hubiera + participle: if only, had
rules.text: Hubiera + participle is the pluperfect subjunctive. It is used for regret and unfulfilled conditions: Ojalá hubiera estudiado más.
rules.because: It is about a wish or condition in the past that did not come true, so hubiera + participle.
examples: I wish I had studied more.
I wish I had not said that.

rules.title: si hubiera…, habría…
rules.text: An unfulfilled condition in the past: si + hubiera + participle, habría + participle.
rules.because: The condition in the past did not come true, so si hubiera + participle and habría + participle.
examples: If I had known, I would have called you.
If we had left earlier, we would have arrived on time.

rules.title: In speech: hubiera in both clauses
rules.text: In casual Mexican speech hubiera is also used in the main clause: Si me hubieras dicho, te hubiera ayudado. It is common and understood.
rules.because: In casual speech hubiera stands in both clauses, in writing the main clause takes habría.
examples: If you had told me, I would have helped you.
If I had arrived earlier, I would have seen him.

title: Conditions: siempre que, a no ser que, por si
intro: Besides si there are other conditional connectors. Most take the subjunctive because they are about something that has not happened yet.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere. “Just in case” is also por si las dudas in casual speech.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere.

rules.title: siempre que, con tal de que + subjunctive
rules.text: Siempre que and con tal de que mean “as long as, provided that” and take the subjunctive: Voy contigo siempre que me invites. In the sense of “whenever” it takes the indicative: Siempre que llueve, me quedo en casa.
rules.because: The condition has not been met yet, so the subjunctive.
examples: I will go with you as long as you invite me.
I will lend you the car provided you take care of it.

rules.title: a no ser que, salvo que + subjunctive
rules.text: A no ser que and salvo que mean “unless” and take the subjunctive: Iremos, a no ser que llueva.
rules.because: The exception is only possible, so the subjunctive.
examples: We will go to the park, unless it rains.
We leave at eight, unless there is traffic.

rules.title: por si (acaso): just in case
rules.text: Por si or por si acaso means “just in case”. The indicative is most common: Llévate un paraguas por si llueve.
rules.because: It is a precaution, so por si.
examples: Take an umbrella in case it rains.
I will leave you my number just in case.

rules.title: como + subjunctive: a threatening condition
rules.text: Como + subjunctive expresses a condition with a threat: Como no vengas, me voy.
rules.because: The condition carries a threat, so como + subjunctive.
examples: If you do not arrive on time, I am leaving.
If you lie to me, I will not speak to you again.

title: Relative clauses and mood: Busco un libro que sea…
intro: After “que” in a relative clause the indicative is used when you know what you mean. If you do not know it or it may not exist, the subjunctive is used.

variants.mx: The same in Mexico as elsewhere.
variants.es: The same in Spain as elsewhere.

rules.title: Known and unknown
rules.text: If you know what you are looking for or have, the indicative is used: Conozco a alguien que habla francés. If it is unknown or hypothetical, the subjunctive is used: Busco a alguien que hable francés.
rules.because: You are looking for something that may not exist, so the subjunctive.
examples: I am looking for a house that has a garden.
I know someone who speaks French.

rules.title: no hay nadie que… + subjunctive
rules.text: After a negation (no hay nadie, no encuentro nada) and in a question (¿hay alguien…?) the next clause takes the subjunctive: No hay nadie que sepa la respuesta.
rules.because: After a negation the thing may not exist, so the subjunctive.
examples: There is nobody who knows the answer.
I cannot find anything I like.

rules.title: A clause between commas: indicative
rules.text: A clause set off by commas only adds information and always takes the indicative: Mi hermana, que vive en Praga, viene mañana.
rules.because: A clause between commas only adds information, so always the indicative.
examples: My sister, who lives in Prague, is coming tomorrow.
The book, which I bought yesterday, is very good.

rules.title: todo lo que, cuanto
rules.text: After todo lo que or cuanto the indicative is used for a known thing and the subjunctive for a wish or the future: Haz todo lo que puedas.
rules.because: The choice depends on a known thing (indicative) or a wish (subjunctive).
